title: How to Resolve Merge Conflicts in Git
content:
1. WHY MERGE CONFLICTS HAPPEN

  • Take example repo: "cal.com"

  • Open source contribution happens through Issues.

  • Two issues created on the same repository, both pointing to the SAME line
    (example: line 32).

    Issue 1: Rename variable "c" to "a"
    Issue 2: Change value of variable "c" (from 40 to 25)

  • Both issues point to the same line -> this is the root cause of conflict.

  1. PRACTICAL EXAMPLE SETUP

  • Two issues created on GitHub:
    Issue 1: Rename the variable c to a
    Issue 2: Change the value of c to 25

  • Since one person is the only contributor, both issues are worked on
    independently, on separate branches.

  1. RESOLVING ISSUE 1 (Rename c to a)

Steps:

  • git pull (update local repo with latest changes)
  • git checkout -b rename-c-to-a (create new branch)
  • Make the change: rename c to a
  • git add .
  • git commit -m "rename c to a"
  • git push
  • Create Pull Request on GitHub
  • Result: No conflicts. PR merged successfully.
  • Issue closed manually (already resolved).
  1. RESOLVING ISSUE 2 (Change value of c to 25)

Steps:

  • git checkout -b fix-change-value-to-25
  • Change value of c to 25
  • git add .
  • git commit -m "change the value to 25"
  • git push
  • Try to create Pull Request
  • Result: CONFLICT appears.

WHY CONFLICT HAPPENED:

  • Issue 1 already merged -> variable renamed from c to a
  • Issue 2 branch still has old code with "c = 25"
  • GitHub is confused: should it take "a = old value" or "c = 25"?
  • It does not know which change to accept.
  1. UNDERSTANDING THE CONFLICT MARKERS

GitHub shows conflict using:

  • A branch name marker
  • A divider line
  • Another marker for the second branch

This means Git is confused between two competing changes:

  • c = 25 (incoming change)
  • a = 40 (current change, already merged)
  1. WRONG WAY TO RESOLVE (must avoid)
  • Simply deleting the conflict markers without thinking does technically
    "resolve" the conflict marker, but it is NOT a good practice.
  • Blindly clicking "Accept Incoming Change" or "Accept Current Change"
    without checking surrounding code can break the code in production.
  1. CORRECT / SMART WAY TO RESOLVE
  • Always check the surrounding code first.
  • In this case, surrounding code uses variable "a" (after rename).
  • So variable name "a" must be kept.
  • But the actual task (issue 2) was to change value to 25.
  • Correct resolution: keep variable name "a" AND apply value 25.
  • Final result: a = 25
  • This combines both changes intelligently instead of blindly picking one side.

Key point: Do not just remove conflict markers randomly. Understand the logic
of both changes and merge them sensibly using common sense.

  1. STEPS AFTER RESOLVING CONFLICT (When PR is already open)

  • git add (or git add .)

  • git rebase --continue

  • Enter commit message if asked

  • git status (confirm everything is clean)

  • git push --force (force push required because PR was already open)

  • After this, check GitHub -> PR shows "No conflicts" -> ready to merge.

Note: Force push is required ONLY because the Pull Request was already open
before the conflict was resolved.

  1. SECOND SCENARIO - CONFLICT WITHOUT AN OPEN PR

Example:

  • Local machine: value changed to 26, but NOT pushed, NOT PR created (only
    local change).
  • Meanwhile, main repository (upstream) changed directly: value changed to 30.

What happens:

  • If you try to push directly, conflict will appear (same as before).
  • But since no PR was open yet, it is a different case.

Correct approach:

  • First run: git pull (get latest changes from upstream)
  • Conflict appears locally (normal merge conflict).
  • Resolve it: check current change (30) vs incoming change (26).
  • Decide based on logic: keep the current change (30) since it came from main
    intentionally.
  • Accept Current Change.
  • git add .
  • git rebase --continue
  • git status -> shows nothing pending
  • git push is NOT required to be forced here, since no PR existed and local
    had no unique unpublished changes needing force.
  1. TWO SCENARIOS OF CONFLICT RESOLUTION - SUMMARY

Scenario 1: Conflict occurs when Pull Request is ALREADY open.
-> Requires git push --force after resolving.

Scenario 2: Conflict occurs when Pull Request is NOT yet created (working
locally, doing git pull).
-> No force push required, just resolve and continue normally.

  1. FINAL TAKEAWAYS
  • Merge conflicts happen when two contributors change the same line
    differently.
  • Never blindly accept "current" or "incoming" change without checking
    surrounding code.
  • Always use logical/common sense understanding of both changes before
    resolving.
  • In real/production-level codebases, conflicts can span across 25-100+
    lines, so resolving carefully is critical.
  • Two conflict resolution flows exist depending on whether PR is already
    open or not.

END OF NOTES
(Part of Open Source Bootcamp Series - Day 5)
